articles.title: Trump is closing an asylum loophole legal immigrants have watched others exploit
articles.summary: A tourist visa should not become a Trojan horse for permanent immigration. While Washington has spent years focused on the southern border, one of the most consequential loopholes may begin at a consulate, where someone promises to visit temporarily and later files for asylum to remain. That is why the Trump administration is preparing to revoke the visitor visas of up to 200,000 foreign nationals who later sought asylum. Critics will call this anti-immigrant, but enforcing the terms of a visa defends every immigrant who entered legally and honestly. It is also how the United States protects the integrity of legal immigration. A visitor visa begins with a representation that an applicant is seeking permission to enter the United States temporarily. A B-1 visa permits limited business activities, such as attending meetings or conferences, while a B-2 visa covers tourism, vacations, visits with family or friends and certain medical treatment. articles.title: Trump is dismantling Iran’s war machine, but America still needs an endgame
articles.summary: For nearly half a century, the Islamic Republic of Iran taught Washington to fear confrontation more than Tehran feared attacking American interests. The regime sponsored terrorism, armed proxies, threatened international shipping and targeted U.S. forces while exploiting American fears of "escalation." President Donald Trump has begun to reverse that equation. The latest strikes matter not simply because Iranian radar, air defenses and maritime assets have been destroyed, but because Washington is imposing a principle Tehran understands: aggression will expose and diminish its military power. For a theocracy that built regional influence by convincing adversaries that retaliation was more dangerous than accommodation, this fundamentally changes the balance of fear. The latest confrontation in the Persian Gulf illustrates that change. articles.summary: In the beginning, there was the famous story about the young journalist Gloria Steinem , going undercover in 1963 as a Playboy Bunny, all décolletage and rabbit ears, in order to expose a culture of degradation and misogyny. The Bunny episode is certainly the Steinem anecdote most often cited, but it’s such an early story that it’s just a canary, really, hinting only a little at what would become a lifelong commitment to feminism. Steinem, who died Sept. 2 in her home in New York City at the age of 92 , was an icon of second-wave feminism. As one of the co-founders, in 1971, of both Ms. magazine and, along with many other feminists, the National Women’s Political Caucus, Steinem advocated fiercely and vocally on behalf of women’s rights. She was also involved in the fight for the passage of the Equal Rights Amendment. But she didn’t consider her life as an “ active feminist ” to have started until 1969, when in her mid-30s she attended an abortion speak-out in a church basement. The big picture: Steinem resisted being cast as feminism's singular face, but for six decades she carried its ideas into mainstream America across its second and third waves. Steinem made the personal political: An illegal abortion at 22 preceded decades of fighting first to legalize abortion and then to defend that right. Flashback: Steinem first drew national attention as a journalist in 1963 when she went undercover as a Playboy Bunny and exposed the job's low pay and sexist treatment.
